synthesis.title: PROFESSOR'S DOCTRINAL SYNTHESIS — THE LAW OF OFFER (NIGERIA)
synthesis.general_principle: A contract in Nigerian law is not made by agreement in the abstract but by a demonstrable sequence: an offer by one party, an unqualified acceptance of that offer by the other, and consideration (plus intention to create legal relations, capacity, certainty and legality where the particular transaction requires them). The offer is the first ingredient, and where there is no offer there is no contract — a proposition the uploaded textbook states and which the Nigerian Supreme Court restates in Sparkling Breweries and Dahiru. The modern Nigerian formulation treats the offer as an expression of readiness to contract on specified terms which, if accepted, produces a binding contract; acceptance is what converts the offer into that contract. The controlling question in every case is therefore not 'was there a bargain?' but 'was a definite, communicated proposal made, and was it accepted without variation?'
constituent_rules: Definition and direction. An offer is made by the offeror to the offeree; it must be communicated, because an uncommunicated offer cannot be accepted (Agomo v Guinness). It may be made to one person, to a defined class, or to the world at large (Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co [1893] 1 QB 256), and it may be express or inferred from conduct.

Definiteness and finality. The proposition must be definite, certain, unequivocal and final, amounting to a definite promise to be bound on specified terms (Tejumola; UBN v Sax). A proposal that leaves a fundamental term open is not an offer at all, because nothing capable of acceptance exists.

Completeness of essential terms. What is 'essential' depends on the transaction: for a lease, the parties, the property, the term, the rent and the date of commencement (Tejumola). For a loan, the amount, repayment period, interest and security (Sax). For a sale of land, the price (Sax's reading of Adebanjo).

Intention to be bound, tested objectively. Whether the offeror intended to be bound is judged from outward words and conduct, not internal intention (Storer). 'Subject to contract' negates present intention and keeps the matter in negotiation (Tejumola).

Offer distinguished from invitation to treat. Advertisements of goods, price lists, display of goods, auction advertisements, invitations to tender and most company prospectuses are invitations to treat, not offers. The distinction is not one of labels but of whether the maker has finally committed himself.

Acceptance must mirror the offer. Acceptance must be final, unqualified and without variance; a reply that adds, subtracts or alters a term is a counter-offer, operates as a rejection, and destroys the original offer (Dahiru; Hyde v Wrench (1840) 3 Beav 334).

Formality is a separate question. A perfectly formed offer and acceptance may still be unenforceable for want of writing (Law Reform (Contracts) Law Cap 66, Laws of Lagos State, s 5) or of the Governor's consent under the Land Use Act.
limits_exceptions_presumptions: The definiteness requirement is not an excuse for the court to destroy bargains: a term may be sufficiently certain if a standard, a course of dealing or an objective yardstick supplies its content. Courts strive to uphold bargains that are complete in substance.
A term is not implied merely because the transaction would work better with it (Sax).
'Subject to contract' is a construction, not an incantation: if the parties' conduct shows a concluded agreement, the label will not defeat it (contrast Storer with Tejumola).

Estoppel can bar a party from denying an arrangement it allowed the other to rely on, even where no contract was formed (Adebanjo) — but estoppel bars inconsistent conduct; it does not create a contract.
The parol evidence rule excludes extrinsic evidence to add to, vary or contradict a written agreement (Sax), subject to the recognised exceptions.

An offer lapses on rejection, on revocation communicated before acceptance, on expiry of a prescribed time or after a reasonable time, on the failure of a condition precedent, or on the death or insanity of the offeror where personal performance is contemplated.
conflicting_or_contrasting_cases: Storer v Manchester City Council [1974] 1 WLR 1403 (CA) — no 'subject to contract' label; detailed letter plus signed return of the agreement created a binding contract.

Gibson v Manchester City Council [1979] 1 WLR 294 (HL) — language of 'may be prepared to sell' was not an offer; the House of Lords distinguished Storer and applied the objective construction of the correspondence. Together the two cases show that the outcome turns on the language actually used, not on sympathy or on political change.
UBA v Tejumola (1988) 2 NWLR (Pt 79) 662 (SC) — 'subject to contract' label plus an unagreed commencement date; no contract, notwithstanding heavy reliance expenditure.
Adebanjo v Brown (1990) 3 NWLR (Pt 141) 661 (SC) — negotiations plus part-performance; still no contract, but estoppel barred the plaintiff.

The four together produce the practical spectrum: no label and full certainty → contract (Storer); no label but a cardinal term missing → no contract, possible estoppel (Adebanjo); label present → no contract, whatever the expense (Tejumola).
binding_status_in_nigeria: Binding (Supreme Court of Nigeria): Sparkling Breweries (2001), Dahiru v Kamale (2005), UBN v Sax (1994), Adebanjo v Brown (1990), UBA v Tejumola (1988), Agomo v Guinness (1995). These bind the Court of Appeal and the High Courts.

Persuasive only (English authority): Storer v Manchester City Council is a decision of the English Court of Appeal. It is of high persuasive value in Nigeria — Nigerian courts routinely adopt English contract doctrine where no local statute or Supreme Court decision displaces it — but it is not binding. Never cite it as if it were a Nigerian decision.

Persuasive only (English authority): Eccles v Bryant and Pollock [1948] Ch 93, Bigg v Boyd Gibbins Ltd [1971] 1 WLR 26, Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co [1893] 1 QB 256, Hyde v Wrench (1840) 3 Beav 334, Nesham v Selby (1872) 7 Ch App 406.
Statute: the Law Reform (Contracts) Law Cap 66 is a Lagos State law. Do not state it as federal law or assume it applies in every State.
statutory_provisions: Law Reform (Contracts) Law, Cap 66, Laws of Lagos State, s 5 — writing requirement; reproduced in Tejumola. Applies to Lagos transactions within its terms.
Land Use Act, Cap L5, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria 2004, s 22 — Governor's consent to the alienation of a statutory or customary right of occupancy; pleaded in Dahiru, not decided there.

Statute of Frauds (1677) (England) — of historical and comparative relevance only; its Nigerian successors are the State Contracts Laws. Its relationship to formation was explained in Bristol, Cardiff and Swansea Aerated Bread Co v Maggs (1890) 44 Ch D 616 at 622, quoted in Tejumola.

Note for the student: always identify the State whose Contracts Law is in issue, and check whether the statute has been re-enacted or amended. A repealed or State-specific provision must not be presented as general Nigerian law.
problem_question_method: Step 1 — Identify the parties and the alleged contract. Who says a contract exists, and on what terms?

Step 2 — Locate the first communication. Was it an offer or an invitation to treat? Apply the objective test from Storer and ask whether the maker had finally committed himself on all essential terms.

Step 3 — Test definiteness. List the essential terms for this type of transaction (lease: PPTRC; loan: APRIS; sale of land: parties, property, price, completion) and check whether each is fixed or capable of being fixed.
Step 4 — Look for a 'subject to contract' or 'subject to' formula and construe it in context (Tejumola; contrast Storer).
Step 5 — Examine the response. Is it an unqualified acceptance, a request for information, a conditional acceptance, or a counter-offer? Apply the mirror-image rule (Dahiru; Hyde v Wrench).
Step 6 — Check communication of acceptance, the mode prescribed (if any), and the timing rules.
Step 7 — Consider formality: writing (State Contracts Law) and consent (Land Use Act) where land is involved.
Step 8 — If no contract, ask whether estoppel, part performance or restitution supplies a remedy (Adebanjo; Tejumola's closing remarks).
Step 9 — State the conclusion conditionally where a fact is missing. Never announce a single outcome that depends on an unproved fact.

questions.disclaimer: These are practice questions written for a 200-level Nigerian law student. They are not predictions of any examination, and the answer guides are outlines, not model answers.

theory.q: 1. 'An offer is the first ingredient to look out for in ascertaining whether there is a contract or not. Where there is no offer, there is no contract.' Discuss this statement with reference to the definitions of an offer in Sparkling Breweries Ltd v Union Bank of Nigeria Ltd and Agomo v Guinness (Nig) Ltd, and explain why the distinction between an offer and an invitation to treat matters in practice.

2. Compare Storer v Manchester City Council with UBA Ltd v Tejumola & Sons Ltd. Why did the English Court of Appeal find a contract in the one case and the Nigerian Supreme Court find none in the other, when in both cases the parties had gone to considerable expense?

3. Examine the requirement that an offer must be 'definite, certain, unequivocal and final'. Using UBN Ltd v Sax (Nig) Ltd and UBA v Tejumola, explain how a Nigerian court decides whether a missing term is fundamental or merely administrative.

4. 'A qualified acceptance is simply a counter-offer and does not give rise to a binding contract.' Critically evaluate this proposition in the light of Dahiru v Kamale and the common law mirror-image rule, and consider whether the rule operates harshly in commercial negotiations.

5. To what extent is Storer v Manchester City Council binding on a Nigerian High Court? Discuss the status of English authorities in Nigerian contract law and the weight a Nigerian court should give to Gibson v Manchester City Council in the light of Storer.

6. Analyse the relationship between the formation of a contract and its enforceability, using the writing requirement in section 5 of the Law Reform (Contracts) Law of Lagos State and the decision in UBA v Tejumola. Does the law's insistence on formality defeat justice?

7. 'Adebanjo v Brown shows that a party may be bound by an arrangement that never became a contract.' Discuss the doctrine of estoppel by election in the context of inconclusive negotiations, and explain its limits.

8. The uploaded page attributes a definition of an offer to Ogbuagu JSC in Dahiru v Kamale [2005] 9 NWLR (Pt 929) 50. Explain, as a matter of research method, why a student should not rely on a citation simply because a textbook prints it, and identify the errors on that page.

problems.q: 1. Bello advertises in a national newspaper: 'For sale: my property at Plot 14, GRA. Serious buyers only. Price negotiable.' Ada writes offering N12 million. Bello replies: 'N12 million is not acceptable. The least I can take is N15 million.' Ada then writes: 'I accept your offer of N12 million.' Bello refuses to sell. Advise Ada.

2. Chief Okoro, wishing to let his warehouse, writes to Delta Logistics Ltd: 'Subject to contract, I offer you the warehouse at 4 Refinery Road for five years at N4 million a year, rent reviewable every two years. Kindly confirm.' Delta replies the same day confirming all the terms and adding: 'We shall take possession on 1 March.' Chief Okoro then spends N3 million on repairs at Delta's request and pays for a structural survey. In June Chief Okoro writes withdrawing. Delta sues for breach of contract. Advise Delta.

3. Musa, a tenant, receives a letter from his local council: 'The council may be prepared to sell your house to you. If you wish to proceed, complete the enclosed application form.' Musa completes and returns the form. The council, after a change of political control, refuses to proceed. Musa sues for specific performance, relying on Storer. Advise Musa, distinguishing Storer.

4. Tunde, a landlord, and Ngozi, a bank, exchange emails over four months about a proposed ten-year lease. They agree on the premises, the rent and the break clause, but never fix the commencement date because Ngozi says it depends on when her current branch closes. Ngozi pays for renovations and Tunde pays for a valuation. Ngozi then pulls out. Advise Tunde, considering both contract and estoppel.

5. Emeka agrees orally to sell his land in Lagos to Fatima for N8 million. Fatima pays N3 million and takes possession, builds a fence and a gatehouse. Emeka later denies any agreement, and no written memorandum exists. Advise Fatima, dealing with the writing requirement, part performance, the Land Use Act and estoppel.

6. A university circular announces: 'Following restructuring, the University intends to re-engage not fewer than 300 of the staff recently disengaged.' Chidi, who was disengaged three months earlier and had collected his terminal benefits, writes accepting 'the offer of re-engagement'. The university refuses to reinstate him. Advise Chidi, using Agomo v Guinness (Nig) Ltd.

answer_guides.T1: Issue: is the offer truly the threshold requirement, and how do Nigerian courts define it? Authority: Sparkling Breweries (2001) per Ogbuagu JSC — an expression of readiness to contract on specified terms which, if accepted, gives rise to a binding contract; Agomo v Guinness (1995) — a proposition put to another coupled with an intimation of willingness to be bound; Tejumola (1988) — offer must be final and unconditional. Explanation: contrast offer with invitation to treat (display of goods, advertisements of goods, price lists, auctions, tenders), and show the practical consequence: an invitation to treat can be withdrawn without liability, an offer once accepted creates a contract. Application: use one short example of each. Conclusion: the statement is accurate as a description of the order of analysis, but note that a court sometimes reaches the same result through the language of certainty or intention rather than the label 'offer'.
answer_guides.T2: Issue: why did outcome differ? Structure: facts of each briefly; then the two distinguishing features — (i) presence of the 'subject to contract' formula in Tejumola and its absence in Storer; (ii) in Storer the council's own letter defined the act of acceptance ('sign and return, and we will send our counterpart') and the only blank was administrative, whereas in Tejumola an essential term (commencement date) was never agreed and was tied to an uncertain contingency. Add the policy point from Tejumola: expense and reliance do not create a contract; Obaseki JSC's 'hard cases make bad law' remark and his call for reform. Conclusion: expense is relevant to estoppel and restitution, not to formation.
answer_guides.T3: Issue: how is 'fundamental' distinguished from 'administrative'? Rule: Sax — fundamental terms must be provided for; a term is not implied for convenience; the court will not make a contract for the parties. Tejumola — the essential terms of a lease are PPTRC and the commencement date is not administrative. Adebanjo — the price of land is fundamental. Counterpoint: Storer — a blank commencement date was administrative because the mechanism of the scheme made it so. Test to state: does the missing term go to the substance of what was promised, so that the parties cannot be said to have committed themselves, or is it merely mechanical? Then apply: the less standardised the transaction and the larger the sum, the more likely a missing term is fundamental.
answer_guides.T4: Issue: does the mirror-image rule operate absolutely? Rule: Dahiru — offer, unqualified acceptance and consideration; a qualified acceptance is a counter-offer. Common law: Hyde v Wrench — counter-offer kills the original offer. Evaluation points: the rule gives certainty and protects the offeror; but it can defeat the reasonable expectations of parties who are in substance agreeing (the 'battle of the forms' problem, and the use of conduct and waiver to retreat from strictness). Note that a mere request for information is not a counter-offer (Stevenson v McLean (1880) 5 QBD 346) — a distinction worth drawing. Conclusion: the proposition is correct as a general rule but is subject to the court's willingness to find acceptance in conduct and to the doctrine of estoppel.
answer_guides.T5: Issue: weight of English authority. Answer: post-1960, English decisions are of persuasive, not binding, authority in Nigeria; Nigerian courts apply common-law doctrine as received and as developed by the Supreme Court. Storer is therefore highly persuasive but a Nigerian court is free to decline it. Gibson (HL) is even more persuasive in hierarchy but rests on different words; the two cases are consistent once the language of the correspondence is examined. Conclusion: a Nigerian court would follow the reasoning of Storer where the facts are truly parallel and no Nigerian authority conflicts, but must treat Tejumola as binding where the facts include a 'subject to contract' formula.
answer_guides.T6: Issue: formation versus enforceability. Answer: formation is governed by common-law offer and acceptance; enforceability of certain contracts is governed by statute (s 5, Cap 66, Lagos). Tejumola shows the two are independent: Kay J's dictum in Bristol, Cardiff and Swansea Aerated Bread Co v Maggs at 622 (quoted in Tejumola) is that whether letters are a complete contract or mere steps in negotiation is independent of the Statute of Frauds. Evaluation: the requirement prevents fabricated claims but can defeat genuine oral bargains; the mitigations are part performance, estoppel, and restitution. Obaseki JSC's warning that the statute is a shield against frauds and not an instrument of frauds is the key quotation. Conclusion: the requirement is defensible in land transactions if the equitable mitigations are kept alive.
answer_guides.T7: Issue: can a party be bound without a contract? Answer: yes, in the sense that estoppel bars inconsistent conduct. Elements from Adebanjo: knowledge of the right, an unequivocal act or representation, and detrimental reliance; the trial judge's finding, upheld by the Supreme Court, that all the ingredients of estoppel by election were present. Limits: estoppel does not supply terms or create a contract; it does not give a right to damages for breach; and it must be pleaded and proved. Contrast with Tejumola, where the expenditure was incurred in the hope of a contract rather than on the faith of a representation.
answer_guides.T8: Issue: research method and accuracy. Answer: three verifiable errors on the page — (i) Dahiru v Kamale begins at page 8 of (2005) 9 NWLR (Pt 929), not 50; (ii) the quotation attributed to Ogbuagu JSC in Dahiru is verbatim the passage reported from Sparkling Breweries Ltd v Union Bank of Nigeria Ltd (2001) 15 NWLR (Pt 737) 539, which the page's own footnote 4 cites; (iii) Agomo v Guinness is at (1995) 2 NWLR (Pt 380) 672, not Pt 580. Method lesson: trace every citation to at least one primary source, verify that the case cited is the case whose report you have opened, and record uncertainty rather than silently correcting. Note the difference between a textbook statement and a verified holding.
answer_guides.P1: Issue: is there a contract between Bello and Ada? Step 1: the advertisement is an invitation to treat, not an offer (advertisement of goods/property for sale; contrast Carlill, where the advertisement itself promised a reward). Step 2: Ada's letter offering N12 million is the offer. Step 3: Bello's reply naming N15 million is a counter-offer, which operates as a rejection of Ada's offer (Hyde v Wrench; Dahiru). Step 4: Ada's purported 'acceptance' of N12 million is therefore an acceptance of an offer that no longer exists; it can only be a fresh offer, which Bello has not accepted. Conclusion: no contract; Ada has no claim in contract. Note that if Bello's letter had merely invited Ada to improve her offer without rejecting it, the analysis could differ. Marks: invitation to treat 5; offer and counter-offer 8; conclusion 4; authority and clarity 3.
answer_guides.P2: Issue: was a binding lease concluded? Step 1: the letter is expressly 'subject to contract' — Tejumola applies and the matter remains in negotiation. Step 2: the commencement date is not fixed but expressed by reference to an event; Tejumola and Obaseki JSC's 'contingency' dictum. Step 3: Delta's reply does not mirror the offer — it adds a possession date, which is a counter-offer. Step 4: expenditure and surveys are reliance, not formation; consider estoppel (Adebanjo) but distinguish: Chief Okoro never represented that a contract existed, and the 'subject to contract' formula negates such a representation. Conclusion: no contract; Delta's claim for breach fails. Advise on possible restitution. Note the contrast with Storer for the absence of the label.
answer_guides.P3: Issue: did the council make an offer? Step 1: distinguish Storer, where the letter said 'if you will sign and return, I will send the agreement signed on behalf of the corporation' — a present commitment. Here the words are 'may be prepared to sell', which are conditional and procedural. Step 2: Gibson v Manchester City Council (HL) is directly in point and is the correct analogy; Musa's completion of the form is an offer, which the council has not accepted. Step 3: consider whether the change of political control is relevant — it is not, save as context. Conclusion: no contract; Musa is not entitled to specific performance. Advice: check whether any Nigerian statute or scheme confers a right independently of contract.
answer_guides.P4: Issue: contract or estoppel? Step 1: no 'subject to contract' label, so Storer applies — look for a concluded contract on the objective construction of the emails. Step 2: the commencement date is treated by Ngozi as contingent on her branch closing, an uncertain event; Tejumola holds that a term left to an uncertain contingency is not agreed. Step 3: consequently there is no complete agreement on an essential term and no contract. Step 4: estoppel — Tunde's expenditure was incurred at Ngozi's request and in the expectation of a lease; consider whether Ngozi made a representation that only a formal document was outstanding. Adebanjo suggests estoppel may bar Ngozi from resiling, but it gives no damages for breach; consider restitution of the valuation cost. Conclusion: state the outcome conditionally on whether a clear representation was made.
answer_guides.P5: Issue: enforceability of an oral land contract. Step 1: formation — offer, acceptance and consideration are present, and part payment plus possession is evidence of them. Step 2: enforceability — s 5 of the Law Reform (Contracts) Law (Lagos) requires writing signed by the party to be charged; there is none, so the contract is not enforceable by action. Step 3: mitigations — the doctrine of part performance (acts unequivocally referable to the contract, such as taking possession and building) may take the case out of the section in equity; consider also proprietary estoppel, which may give a right to a charge or compensation rather than to the land. Step 4: the Land Use Act — a transfer without the Governor's consent is invalid; consider whether the consent requirement prevents specific performance or whether an order can be made conditional on consent. Conclusion: Fatima's best route is part performance and estoppel; specific performance is unlikely to be granted unconditionally. Note that the outcome depends on facts not given, and say so.
answer_guides.P6: Issue: was the circular an offer? Step 1: the circular is an internal statement of intention ('intends to re-engage not fewer than 300'), addressed to no identified offeree and committing the university to no one — directly analogous to the internal directive in Agomo, which was held not to be an offer. Step 2: Chidi is in any event outside the class, having ceased to be an employee when he took his terminal benefits (Agomo). Step 3: distinguish Carlill — there the advertisement itself promised a reward to anyone who performed the stipulated act. Step 4: consider whether any statute (for example the Labour Act or the university's own statute) gives an independent right, and whether the termination was merely wrongful or void. Conclusion: no contract of re-engagement; Chidi's claim in contract fails.

oral_test: 1. Give the citation of Storer and name the court and the judge who delivered the leading judgment.
2. In one sentence, what did Tejumola decide about the words 'subject to contract'?
3. What are the five essential terms of an agreement for a lease identified in Tejumola?
4. State the counter-offer rule and name one Nigerian and one English authority for it.
5. What did Adebanjo decide about the effect of negotiation and expense?
6. Correct these citations: 'Dahiru v Kamale [2005] 9 NWLR (Pt 929) 50' and 'Agomo v Guinness (Nig) Plc [1995] 2 NWLR (Pt 580) 672'.
7. Which case in this casebook is a decision of the English Court of Appeal, and why does that matter?
8. What fact would have changed the result in Tejumola? Answer in one line.
